name: Mali
card_headline: Mali's army retook Kidal with Russian help in October, six months after a jihadist and Tuareg offensive killed the defence minister and cost it Kidal
card_summary: Colonel Assimi Goita's military government is fighting JNIM, al-Qaeda's Sahel affiliate, and the Tuareg-led FLA. Their coordinated attacks of 25 April killed Defence Minister Sadio Camara. [1] The army and Russia's Africa Corps re-entered Kidal on 6 October, though the FLA calls its exit a controlled withdrawal. [2] Reuters sources say JNIM killed more than 100 soldiers at Dioura in September. [3] About 415,000 people are displaced. [4]
card_local: Local sourcing is thin in this draft. The Malian weekly L'Alternance pressed for restoring political parties in February, and its publisher Youssouf Sissoko was later sentenced to two years over an unrelated commentary. [5][6]
card_international: AFP and Reuters report the army's October return to Kidal, the September attack at Dioura and the strain on Russia's Africa Corps. [2][3]
card_scholar: Chatham House, ICCT and GI-TOC read the April offensive as a JNIM and FLA alliance that force alone has not beaten, and Crisis Group warned in January of a growing risk of regime collapse. [7][8][9][10]
context_md: Colonel Assimi Goita took power in coups in 2020 and 2021. [11] The junta turned to Russia, first the Wagner Group and since June 2025 the state-controlled Africa Corps. [2] Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formed the Alliance of Sahel States, and Mali left ECOWAS. [12] The junta dissolved all political parties in May 2025 and in July 2025 gave Goita a five-year term renewable without an election. [11][12] JNIM, formed in 2017, has fought the state for years and began a fuel blockade of Bamako in September 2025. [8][13] On 25 April 2026 the Tuareg-led FLA and JNIM launched coordinated attacks across the country. [8][1]

sections.title: The 25 April offensive: JNIM and the FLA hit Kati, Bamako and the north at once
sections.body_md:
On 25 April 2026 JNIM and the Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) struck the army base at Kati, the area near Bamako's airport and towns in the north and centre. [1][14] Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed. Chatham House describes a suicide vehicle bomb at his home and reports the intelligence chief gravely injured. [7] Al Jazeera calls the attacks the largest in nearly 15 years, and the Long War Journal's Caleb Weiss calls them the largest coordinated offensive in Mali since 2012. [1][15]

The north fell fast. GI-TOC reports that the FLA and JNIM took Kidal on 25 April, then Tessalit and Tessit, with the army and Africa Corps mostly negotiating surrenders or withdrawing. It adds that the FLA claims 80 percent of the Kidal region. [9] Chatham House says about 400 Russian Africa Corps fighters left Kidal and abandoned vehicles. [7] In the south the government held: GI-TOC says forces in Bamako and Kati largely repelled the attackers and kept the airport. On 28 April JNIM announced a blockade of Bamako, and by 1 May it was reported to have set up checkpoints around the capital. [9][16]

Who stands behind it matters. Wassim Nasr of ICCT writes that JNIM and the FLA began talks in early 2025 and reportedly agreed to govern recaptured cities jointly, with the FLA in the lead administrative role. He argues the junta's repression pushed varied actors toward cooperation. [8] Chatham House warns the alliance may be fragile because the FLA seeks autonomy or independence while JNIM seeks a national government under Sharia. [7] Mali's army said in May that the attacks aimed to assassinate Goita. The claim was reported without independent verification. [17]

lenses.local: No Malian outlet reporting on the April attacks was read for this draft. The army's account reached readers through an army spokesperson at a press conference. [17]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, AFP and Reuters report the attacks as the largest in nearly 15 years. Russia's Defence Ministry says its forces helped stop a coup, which Al Jazeera could not verify. [1]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House and ICCT read the offensive as an alliance of groups with different aims, and both call for negotiation alongside military pressure. [7][8]

sections.title: Kidal retaken in October, but the front is long and the losses keep coming
sections.body_md:
On 6 October the army said it had entered Kidal after air and ground operations backed by Africa Corps. A statement carried by state television said troops had consolidated their positions with their Russian partners. The FLA announced a strategic and controlled withdrawal and blamed Russian air power, and AFP and Reuters report that the army entered without a fight. [2] Control Risks analyst Beverly Ochieng said the recapture would lift army morale but is largely symbolic. [2]

A month later RFI's David Baché reported that the army holds Kidal, Anéfis and Aguelhok but has not advanced to Tessalit or Tinzaouatène. Kidal is largely depopulated and the civil administration has not returned. An analyst quoted by RFI calls the army's supply line long and exposed. On 5 November the FLA claimed drone strikes on Africa Corps and Malian forces at Anéfis, and an FLA official told RFI it is a long war. [18]

Losses elsewhere continue. Reuters, citing a security source, reports that 130 soldiers died in the 10 September attack on the Dioura camp in central Mali and that more than 100 were taken hostage. A diplomatic source put the toll near 120, and JNIM claimed 150. The army acknowledged losses without a figure. [3] On 18 July, HRW says, JNIM and FLA fighters ambushed an army convoy in the Gao region and tortured and executed at least 19 captured soldiers. JNIM acknowledges that prisoners were killed but denies ordering it, and the FLA denies executing soldiers. [19] RFI adds that the Islamic State Sahel branch killed about 50 civilians in the Ménaka region in the previous month. [18]

lenses.local: A resident of Sévaré told Reuters of six consecutive nights of shelling at the airport and about 40 wounded Malian soldiers and Russian fighters at the hospital. [3]
lenses.international: Reuters, AFP and RFI carry the casualty counts. The army's own statements are the main official record and give no figures. [3][2]
lenses.scholar: ICCT's Nasr notes that Africa Corps could not hold every front and negotiated withdrawals from several northern towns, but expects the Russia partnership to deepen. [8]

sections.title: The fuel blockade has eased in Bamako, but supply and gold output stay fragile
sections.body_md:
JNIM began a fuel blockade in early September 2025. By November Reuters reported it had lasted about two months, and diplomats and analysts it quoted believed the aim was to provoke another coup. [13] Crisis Group wrote in January that the militants wanted to pressure the military and tighten their rural hold, not to seize the capital, and warned that the risk of regime collapse was growing. [10] The IMF said in December that fuel disruption from terrorist attacks was the immediate economic priority. [20]

After the April offensive JNIM announced a renewed blockade of Bamako. [9] RFI reported on 3 September that more than 900 tankers under military escort reached the capital on 30 August, according to the DGCC, that queues had disappeared, and that power cuts that once ran up to 15 hours a day had eased. Outside Bamako supply stayed uneven: Mopti had about five hours of electricity a day, fuel in Bandiagara came from the black market, and Koro and Bankass had near-continuous outages for months. [21]

Gold is the other pressure point. Mali agreed to a 10-year permit renewal for Barrick's Loulo-Gounkoto complex after a long dispute, and Semafor, citing Reuters, says the complex earned almost $900 million in 2024. [22] Reuters later reported that the complex produced about 80,000 ounces in the first quarter of 2026, that Barrick left the Gounkoto mine out of its 2026 plans, and that its largest contractor was closing its Mali operations and laying off more than 600 workers. The same report says Mali's gold output fell 23 percent in 2025. [23] The IMF's second program review in March found all quantitative targets met and consumer prices rising by less than 3 percent in 2025. [24] In December it had projected growth of 4.1 percent in 2025 and 5.5 percent in 2026, a forecast made before the April offensive. [20]

lenses.local: Residents quoted by RFI say fuel is available in Bamako and the long queues have gone, while Mopti, Bandiagara, Koro and Bankass remain short. [21]
lenses.international: Reuters covers the blockade's economic effects and the Barrick contractor exit, relying partly on unnamed sources. [13][23]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group and GI-TOC read the blockade as pressure on the junta. GI-TOC names artisanal gold, especially the N'Tahaka mine, as a likely priority revenue source in the new conflict economy. [10][9]

sections.title: Russia's Africa Corps is the junta's main backer, and its record is in doubt
sections.body_md:
Africa Corps replaced the Wagner Group in June 2025 and answers directly to Russia's Defence Ministry. [2] After the April attacks the ministry said its forces helped stop a rebel coup aimed at the presidential palace and other key sites, and confirmed that they left Kidal. Al Jazeera could not verify the coup claim. The ministry is a party to the war, so its statements are state-affiliated. [1]

Chatham House says Mali's defence pact with Niger and Burkina Faso has produced little concrete support and that Russia's reliability has been exposed. [7] ICCT's Nasr argues the Russia partnership is more likely to deepen than collapse. [8] GI-TOC reports that a Russian military aircraft landed in Bamako on 6 May and that Africa Corps says it will keep fighting alongside the army, with no sign of withdrawal. [9]

Washington has made overtures. ISS researcher Djiby Sow wrote in February that US official Nick Checker visited Bamako to reset ties, and that Mali's reliance on Russia and China limits any shift. He notes that the Goulamina and Bougouni lithium assets are under Chinese control. [25] In July Africanews relayed a Washington Post report that the Trump administration was weighing action against JNIM. Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop said Mali had no confirmation and was not waiting for others to solve its problem. [26]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Africanews carry Russia's coup claim and Mali's rejection of a US role. [1][26]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House, ICCT and ISS agree that Russia's partnership has limits, and differ on whether it will survive them. [7][8][25]

sections.title: A junta with no parties, no election date and a mandate that can run past 2030
sections.body_md:
Goita took power in coups in 2020 and 2021. [11] The military dissolved all political parties on 13 May 2025, after protests on 3 and 4 May. Human rights groups said several politicians had been forcibly disappeared in the days before, and the authorities did not comment on the reported arrests. [11] In July 2025 the transitional council backed a charter giving Goita a five-year term renewable without an election, which would let him lead until at least 2030. Council president Malick Diaw called it a major step forward. The revised charter drops references to political parties. [12]

Reuters reported that the authorities arrested two generals and dozens of soldiers in August 2025 over an alleged plot. [13] Crisis Group counts the party dissolution, the arrest of two former prime ministers and the alleged plot as signs of strain inside the junta. [10] Chatham House says the April attacks damage the junta's legitimacy and could raise a coup threat to Goita. [7] After the attacks Goita was not seen for several days. His office released photos of him with Russian ambassador Igor Gromyko on 28 April, with no statement. [1]

The government's own line is that it is in control. A Malian minister told Al Arabiya, as relayed by APA, that Bamako is not under siege, that the government controls the whole territory and that talks with armed groups are ruled out unless they disarm. The report carries no date, and it is a single-source government statement. [27] Jonathan Guiffard of Institut Montaigne argues instead that a negotiated settlement involving the FLA, JNIM and regional mediators is the most likely path and that Western intervention is unlikely. [28]

lenses.local: L'Alternance, a Malian weekly, ran several pieces in February arguing for the restoration of political parties dissolved in May 2025. [5]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters report the party dissolution, the extended mandate and the alleged August 2025 plot. [11][12][13]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group and Institut Montaigne both point to dialogue as the way out, and Crisis Group says the window for diplomacy is narrowing. [10][28]

sections.title: Civilians and journalists: abuses by the army, Russian forces and armed groups, and a jailed press
sections.body_md:
HRW's October report, drawing on 30 interviews and ACLED data, says the military and its Russian allies killed civilians and armed groups did the same. HRW counts 49 airstrikes by Malian forces and Africa Corps between April and August that killed 89 civilians, against 22 strikes and 44 deaths a year earlier. HRW sent its findings to Mali's defence minister on 5 August and received no reply. [19] In a separate report HRW says more than 100 Africa Corps fighters entered Bombori in Mopti region on 10 July, rounded up at least 80 men and boys, and left nine bodies, four of them children, according to residents. Neither the Malian nor the Russian defence ministry replied. [29] On 22 October HRW described a 16 September drone strike at Guélédié that killed eight men, and detainees held in a shipping container at Sévaré. [30]

Amnesty's report of 29 September documents at least 34 unlawful killings in the Ségou, Mopti and Timbuktu regions between June 2023 and December 2025 by the army and Wagner personnel. Most victims were Fulani, Arab and Tuareg pastoralists. Amnesty says UNHCR had registered 290,000 Malian refugees in Mauritania by 31 July and that Mali had not responded. It also reports that Mali notified its withdrawal from the Rome Statute in June 2026, effective 23 June 2027. [31]

The press is squeezed. CPJ reports that Chahana Takiou of 22 Septembre was ordered arrested on 8 June and Abdrahamane Keïta of Le Témoin detained on 9 June under the 2019 cybercrimes law, after Keïta said on television that JNIM controls Kidal. Youssouf Sissoko received a two-year sentence in March over a commentary about Niger's president. A deputy prosecutor told CPJ that newspaper writing shared on social media can be prosecuted under the law. [6]

lenses.local: Studio Tamani, a Bamako-based radio programme, says restrictions, administrative suspensions and cybercrime detentions grew in 2025, and that sensitive coverage has encouraged self-censorship. Its airtime was cut from 3.5 hours to one hour a day from August 2025. [32]
lenses.international: AFP, via Al Jazeera, carries HRW's findings and the responses of JNIM and the FLA to the convoy allegation. [19]

sections.title: 415,000 displaced, 5.1 million in need and a response plan funded at about 15 percent
sections.body_md:
UNICEF's first-quarter report counts about 415,000 internally displaced people, 58 percent of them children, and nearly 280,000 refugees, mainly from Burkina Faso and Niger. Humanitarian partners estimate 5.1 million people need assistance in 2026, including about 3.2 million children. Nearly 391,000 children under five suffer severe wasting, and 2,374 schools were non-functional in March, up from 2,006 a year earlier, affecting more than 700,000 children. [4] OCHA's regional overview of 29 April also gives 415,000 displaced for Mali. [33]

ACAPS says about 15 percent of the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan was funded by mid-March. It reports that access incidents from January to September 2025 rose nearly 50 percent over the same period in 2024, mostly because of improvised explosive devices. It projects Kidal at IPC phase 3 from March to September 2026 and Ménaka at phase 4 in the lean season, with cereal prices 32 percent above the five-year average in Kidal and 44 percent in Ménaka in February. [14] WFP cites a Cadre Harmonisé projection of about 1.5 million acutely food insecure people in the June to August lean season, and a funding gap of $73.6 million. [34]

After the April attacks ACAPS found no confirmed displacement figures for the north. It notes that the 2023 Kidal operation displaced at least 11,500 people, and that curfews, checkpoints and attacks on transport corridors restrict assessments. [14] RFI says Kidal is largely depopulated and that a vaccination campaign began there in late October. [18]

lenses.international: UNICEF, OCHA and WFP are the main sources on displacement, malnutrition and hunger. [4][33][34]
lenses.scholar: ACAPS finds that curfews, checkpoints and attacks on transport corridors restrict needs assessments after the April offensive. [14]

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AFP and Al Jazeera filed heavily after 25 April and again around the Dioura attack and the Kidal recapture. [1][3][2] Think tanks such as ACAPS, GI-TOC and Chatham House produce steady analysis, but attention is episodic between big events. [14][9][7] Malian outlets are constrained by cybercrime prosecutions of journalists, which thins local reporting. [6]

severity.basis: Coordinated JNIM and FLA attacks killed the defence minister in April, sources report 120 to 130 soldiers dead at Dioura in September, and HRW counts 89 civilians killed in 49 airstrikes from April to August. [1][3][19]
About 415,000 people are displaced, 5.1 million need aid and the response plan was about 15 percent funded in mid-March. [4][14]

Parties were dissolved in May 2025, Goita holds a five-year renewable term, journalists are jailed under the cybercrime law, and HRW and Amnesty document abuses by the army and Africa Corps. [11][12][6][30]
Gold output fell 23 percent in 2025 and the fuel blockade disrupted power and supply, though the IMF found program targets met and inflation under 3 percent. [23][21][24]
The army lost Kidal in April and suffered mass casualties at Dioura in September, but it re-entered Kidal in October and Bamako's fuel supply improved. [1][3][2][21]

parts.basis: Russia's Africa Corps fights alongside the army, a US official visited Bamako in February, and Chinese firms control lithium assets. [2][25]
Gold is the main export story and Mali is projected to become Africa's second-largest lithium producer in 2026, though its trade with the United States is small. [23][25]
The Sahel alliance, JNIM's reach beyond Mali and 290,000 refugees in Mauritania tie the war to its neighbours. [7][31]
About 290,000 Malian refugees are registered in Mauritania, and Mali hosts nearly 280,000 refugees from Burkina Faso and Niger. [31][4]

Mali's notified exit from the Rome Statute and the replacement of Wagner by a state-controlled Africa Corps, after exits from ECOWAS and French forces, reshape who holds armies to account. [31][12][2]

summary: Mali matters beyond its borders through the Sahel war, Russia's military footprint and the movement of refugees, more than through trade. [2][31] Chatham House notes that the Sahel alliance has produced little joint military help, which leaves neighbours exposed to the fallout. [7]
gi.up: A fall or collapse of the Bamako government, or JNIM pushing into Burkina Faso, Niger or coastal states.
gi.down: A negotiated settlement with the FLA and JNIM, or a stable truce along the northern front.

gaps: Local Malian outlets: only two local sources are cited, a weekly's issue of February and a radio programme's project sheet. No Malian reporting on events from April to November was read, and the state broadcaster ORTM was not read directly; its statements reach this draft through AFP and Reuters.
Casualty figures for Dioura rest on unnamed security and diplomatic sources, and JNIM's figure is its own claim. Army and Russian Defence Ministry statements were not independently verified.
No displacement figure after the April offensive exists in the sources read; ACAPS says none was confirmed, and the 415,000 total predates it.
The HRW report of 19 October was read through an Al Jazeera and AFP summary, the Crisis Group paper through an allAfrica copy and the Amnesty report through its press page.
The scholar lens relies on think tanks and NGOs; no peer-reviewed article on the 2026 war was read.
The IMF 5.5 percent growth projection was made in December 2025 and predates the April offensive. No World Bank or updated IMF figure was read.
The APA report quoting a government minister is undated and its outlet was not identified.
JNIM and FLA abuses are covered only through HRW's report as summarised by Al Jazeera.
No documentary or film was verified for the media list. The forthcoming Laessing book is listed from a publisher page and is not yet in print.

reporters.name: Caleb Weiss
reporters.bio: Wrote the 26 April 2026 Long War Journal report on the JNIM and FLA offensive, one day after the attacks.
reporters.why: His report names the towns hit and calls the offensive the largest of its kind in Mali since 2012.
reporters.label: FDD's Long War Journal

reporters.name: Wassim Nasr
reporters.bio: Wrote the 28 May 2026 ICCT Short Read on the reasons for and consequences of the 25 April attacks.
reporters.why: He traces how JNIM and the FLA negotiated their alliance from early 2025.
reporters.label: ICCT

reporters.name: David Baché
reporters.bio: Bylined the RFI reports of 3 September 2026 on Bamako's fuel supply and of 6 November 2026 on the front around Kidal.
reporters.why: His reports give on-the-ground detail on fuel, power and the northern front that wires rarely carry.
reporters.label: RFI via allAfrica

reporters.name: Portia Crowe
reporters.bio: Bylined the Reuters reports of 3 November 2025 on the fuel blockade and of 21 September 2026 on the Dioura attack.
reporters.why: Her September report is the main source on the Dioura toll and the situation in Sévaré and Konna.
reporters.label: Reuters via The Star

reporters.name: Ilaria Allegrozzi
reporters.bio: Named in HRW's 22 October 2026 release as its Sahel researcher, who blamed the junta for failing to restrain its forces and allies.
reporters.why: HRW's work under her area documents civilian harm by the army, Africa Corps and armed groups.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

reporters.name: Youssouf Sissoko
reporters.bio: Listed as founder and publication director of the weekly in its issue of 2 February 2026. CPJ reports a two-year sentence in March 2026 over a commentary about Niger's president.
reporters.why: His case shows the risk Malian editors run under the cybercrime law.
reporters.label: Committee to Protect Journalists

reporters.name: Beverly Ochieng
reporters.bio: Quoted by Al Jazeera on 6 October 2026 on the recapture of Kidal and guest on Al Jazeera's The Take on 30 April 2026.
reporters.why: She assesses what the Kidal recapture changes and what it does not.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

books.author: Joshua Hammer
books.why: Tells how the archivist Abdel Kader Haidara smuggled about 350,000 manuscripts out of Timbuktu as jihadists closed in, according to the publisher.
books.label: Simon & Schuster

books.title: Flames in the Sahel
books.author: Yusuf Gamawa
books.why: Covers the Tuareg struggle for independence, the 2012 revolt and the spread of armed groups across Mali and Burkina Faso, per the publisher's listing.
books.label: Sureshot Books listing

books.title: From Empire to NGOs in the West African Sahel: The Road to Nongovernmentality
books.author: Gregory Mann
books.why: Afropop's 2016 interview names it as the latest book by a Columbia historian of francophone West Africa who has lived extensively in Mali.
books.label: Afropop Worldwide

books.title: The Road to Bamako: Jihadists, Russian Mercenaries and Europe's Defeat in the Sahel
books.author: Ulf Laessing
books.why: A journalist's account of the jihadist advance toward Bamako and Russia's rise in the Sahel. The publisher lists May 2027 as the date, so it is not yet in print.
books.label: University of Chicago Press (distributor)

local_md:
No Malian outlet reporting on the April attacks was read for this draft. The army's account reached readers through an army spokesperson at a press conference. [17]

A resident of Sévaré told Reuters of six consecutive nights of shelling at the airport and about 40 wounded Malian soldiers and Russian fighters at the hospital. [3]

Residents quoted by RFI say fuel is available in Bamako and the long queues have gone, while Mopti, Bandiagara, Koro and Bankass remain short. [21]

L'Alternance, a Malian weekly, ran several pieces in February arguing for the restoration of political parties dissolved in May 2025. [5]

Studio Tamani, a Bamako-based radio programme, says restrictions, administrative suspensions and cybercrime detentions grew in 2025, and that sensitive coverage has encouraged self-censorship. Its airtime was cut from 3.5 hours to one hour a day from August 2025. [32]
international_md:
Al Jazeera, AFP and Reuters report the attacks as the largest in nearly 15 years. Russia's Defence Ministry says its forces helped stop a coup, which Al Jazeera could not verify. [1]

Reuters, AFP and RFI carry the casualty counts. The army's own statements are the main official record and give no figures. [3][2]

Reuters covers the blockade's economic effects and the Barrick contractor exit, relying partly on unnamed sources. [13][23]

Al Jazeera and Africanews carry Russia's coup claim and Mali's rejection of a US role. [1][26]

Al Jazeera and Reuters report the party dissolution, the extended mandate and the alleged August 2025 plot. [11][12][13]

AFP, via Al Jazeera, carries HRW's findings and the responses of JNIM and the FLA to the convoy allegation. [19]

UNICEF, OCHA and WFP are the main sources on displacement, malnutrition and hunger. [4][33][34]
scholar_md:
Chatham House and ICCT read the offensive as an alliance of groups with different aims, and both call for negotiation alongside military pressure. [7][8]

ICCT's Nasr notes that Africa Corps could not hold every front and negotiated withdrawals from several northern towns, but expects the Russia partnership to deepen. [8]

Crisis Group and GI-TOC read the blockade as pressure on the junta. GI-TOC names artisanal gold, especially the N'Tahaka mine, as a likely priority revenue source in the new conflict economy. [10][9]

Chatham House, ICCT and ISS agree that Russia's partnership has limits, and differ on whether it will survive them. [7][8][25]

Crisis Group and Institut Montaigne both point to dialogue as the way out, and Crisis Group says the window for diplomacy is narrowing. [10][28]

ACAPS finds that curfews, checkpoints and attacks on transport corridors restrict needs assessments after the April offensive. [14]
